edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: A fatal Cairo highway fire, new pressure on Israel’s prime minister and a fresh round of US tariffs lead the day. In Britain, EU reset texts are due; Denmark is among the countries financing support for Ukraine.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and consequential reporting. Repeated subjects are included only where this gather brings a significant development or distinct reporting; older or unchanged coverage is left out.

content.headline: US proposes tariffs on 14 trading partners, drawing protests
content.shortHeadline: US tariff proposals draw protests from trading partners
content.standfirst: The proposed duties could take effect next year after consultation. China faces among the highest rates, while Brazil and other affected governments dispute Washington’s case and warn of economic consequences.

image.caption: The US has proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, Japan and the EU.

sources.originalTitle: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless

segments.body: The United States has proposed new import duties on 14 trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan and South Korea. The BBC reports proposed rates of up to 40% for China and 35% for Vietnam; the measures are not expected to take effect until next year and must go through consultation and potentially hearings.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that Brazil condemned the proposal and reserved the possibility of retaliation. It says the US described China’s rate as capped at 20%, though other duties could bring the total on some goods to 45.

segments.body: The US says the measures respond to trade practices it considers unfair. Several governments reject that argument. The European Commission says it will examine the reasons for the tariffs, while China calls the excess-capacity claim a pretext for political manipulation. Economists warn tariffs can raise consumer prices, though one analyst cited by the BBC expects the price effect to be marginal.

content.headline: Cairo tanker crash sparks fire that kills at least 31
content.shortHeadline: Cairo tanker fire kills at least 31
content.standfirst: A fuel tanker crash ignited a large fire on a busy ring road, killing at least 31 people and injuring at least 21, Egyptian authorities say. The prosecutor has opened an investigation; the cause has not been established.

image.caption: A large fire engulfed vehicles after a fuel tanker crashed on a highway near Cairo.

sources.originalTitle: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
Mindst 31 dræbt i brand efter ulykke med tankbil i Egypten

segments.body: At least 31 people were killed and at least 21 injured when a fuel tanker crash caused a fire on Cairo’s ring road on Wednesday, according to Egyptian authorities. The blaze burned nearby vehicles. The health ministry said ambulances took the injured to hospitals, and the public prosecutor is investigating.

Authorities have not established how the crash happened. State media reported that the tanker overturned; BBC reporting also cites a report that a high-voltage cable fell in front of the truck, but that account has not been confirmed by officials. The death toll is described as preliminary and could change.

content.headline: Hong Kong fire report cites failures behind blaze that killed 168
content.shortHeadline: Hong Kong fire report finds a preventable disaster
content.standfirst: A year after the Wang Fuk Court blaze, an independent committee says human errors and safety failures contributed to the fire that killed 168. Families are still seeking answers, and the criminal cases have yet to go to trial.

image.caption: The Wang Fuk Court fire killed 168 people in one of Hong Kong’s deadliest blazes.

sources.originalTitle: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168

segments.body: An independent committee’s report says the fire at Hong Kong’s Wang Fuk Court was preventable, citing human errors, fire-safety failures and suspected corruption. The blaze killed 168 people. Investigators said a cigarette may have started it; the report also described non-fire-retardant replacement netting and complaints that officials largely ignored.

segments.title: Families still waiting
segments.body: The report says the estate’s fire alarms had been switched off and that altered stairwell windows let smoke in, cutting off escape routes. Companies and seven people have been charged with offences including manslaughter and conspiracy to defraud; none of the cases has gone to trial. Hong Kong’s housing chief resigned as the report was released, and the city’s leader apologised and promised reforms.

content.headline: SpaceX wins US approval for plan to launch up to a million data satellites
content.shortHeadline: SpaceX approved to launch up to a million data satellites
content.standfirst: The proposed Starmind network would process data in orbit using solar power, as demand for AI computing grows. The licence sets a timetable for deployment, but it is unclear whether SpaceX will launch the full number approved.

sources.originalTitle: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space

segments.body: US regulators have approved SpaceX’s plan for a constellation of up to one million satellites that would process data for artificial intelligence in orbit and send results to Earth. The company says the solar-powered system could meet growing computing demand more efficiently than ground-based data centres.

The licence requires deployment to begin by November 2033, with 10% of the satellites in orbit by November 2035 and half by November 2038. SpaceX says it wants to launch its first satellite next year, but it is not clear whether it intends to use the full approval. Experts cited by the BBC raise concerns about the cost of launching hardware, space debris and collision risks.

content.headline: Israeli judges urge rethink of corruption cases against Netanyahu
content.shortHeadline: Israeli judges recommend dropping major Netanyahu charges
content.standfirst: Judges have questioned the prospects of conviction in one case and the legal basis of another, while suggesting a plea deal in a third. The attorney general says she will consider their recommendations; Netanyahu denies wrongdoing.

image.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu has called for his corruption trial to end; he denies the allegations.

sources.originalTitle: Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious charges against Netanyahu
Dommer anbefaler at droppe korruptionssag mod Netanyahu

segments.body: A panel at Jerusalem District Court has urged Israel’s attorney general to reconsider the corruption trial of Benjamin Netanyahu. The judges said conviction was unlikely in a case alleging favourable media coverage was exchanged for government benefits, questioned whether conduct in a second case amounted to a crime, and suggested a plea deal in a third.

Netanyahu, who denies all the allegations, called for the trial to end. The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, said she would consider the recommendations. The development comes as Netanyahu’s political rival Gadi Eisenkot attempts to form a government after an inconclusive election; both blocs fell short of a majority.

content.headline: UN tribunal says evidence for sacking Palestinian aid worker was inadequate
content.shortHeadline: UN tribunal questions evidence used to sack Palestinian aid worker
content.standfirst: A UN tribunal says the agency failed to provide evidence supporting the dismissal of one Palestinian employee accused of links to Hamas. It awarded him compensation; the ruling does not determine the broader allegations against the workers.

image.caption: Displaced people receive food from a charity kitchen in southern Gaza.

sources.originalTitle: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules

segments.body: A UN dispute tribunal ruled that the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to dismiss Abu Awad in 2024. The tribunal said the allegations against him appeared to rely almost entirely on information held by Israel and described that material as having limited evidentiary value and reliability.

The tribunal did not decide whether the allegations were true, but awarded Awad a year’s pay and $5,000 in moral damages. It said UNRWA’s supporting documents appeared to have been produced after the dismissal decision. The agency did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment; former commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini said he understood the ruling might be appealed.

content.headline: Somalia faces security risks as foreign forces withdraw and election dispute wid
content.shortHeadline: Somalia’s security tested by troop withdrawals and political crisis
content.standfirst: Al-Shabab remains a threat as foreign forces begin to leave and Somali leaders clash over elections. Analysts disagree on whether the country’s security institutions can manage the transition without greater instability.

image.caption: African Union troops have supported Somalia’s government as it fights al-Shabab.

sources.originalTitle: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?

segments.body: Somalia is facing pressure on several fronts: Ugandan troops have begun withdrawing from the African Union mission, Ethiopia is reportedly considering a pullback, and political divisions are complicating plans for direct elections. Al-Shabab controls large parts of the country, while the government says Somali forces are ready to take on more responsibility.

Analysts warn that Somali forces are stretched by fighting militants and taking over positions vacated by foreign troops. One former security official fears Mogadishu could be vulnerable; another analyst says the staggered withdrawal could test progress in rebuilding the security forces. The dispute over election rules has deepened after the Supreme Court rejected a presidential term extension, a decision the government has since rejected.

Somalia also relies heavily on overseas funding: the finance ministry says donor grants make up two-thirds of the planned 2026 budget, but only about 35% of the expected annual grants had arrived in the first nine months. Whether other partners can replace departing troops and support remains uncertain.

content.headline: Israeli strike kills senior Hamas security official and three family members
content.shortHeadline: Israeli strike kills Hamas security chief and family in Gaza
content.standfirst: Doctors and the Hamas-run interior ministry say Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, his wife and two teenage daughters were killed in Gaza City. Israel says Abu al-Ouf was a militant whose role impeded its operations.

image.caption: The strike damaged the Abu al-Ouf family’s apartment in Gaza City.

sources.originalTitle: Israeli strike kills senior Hamas security official and family in Gaza City

segments.body: An Israeli air strike hit an apartment in Gaza City’s Shati refugee camp at dawn on Wednesday, killing Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, a senior Hamas internal security official, his wife and their two teenage daughters, according to local doctors and the Hamas-run interior ministry.

Israel’s military called Abu al-Ouf a terrorist and said he was a significant figure who helped restrict its counter-terrorism operations. The strike follows another Israeli attack that killed the head of Hamas’s internal security service. Near-daily strikes continue despite a ceasefire agreed last October; casualty figures cited by the report come from the Hamas-run health ministry.

content.headline: UK and EU to publish post-Brexit treaties, including 10-year exit clause
content.shortHeadline: UK-EU treaties due, with 10-year exit clause revealed
content.standfirst: The texts cover food trade and emissions trading, alongside legislation to implement the deals. The reported termination clause could require either side to pay towards rebuilding border-check infrastructure if it withdraws.

sources.originalTitle: UK government set to publish new treaties agreed with EU

segments.body: The UK and EU are due to publish two treaties on Thursday afternoon, covering food trade and emissions trading, with legislation to implement the agreements. The food deal is intended to reduce paperwork and checks for exporters; an internal assessment cited by the BBC forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.

The BBC understands the treaties include a 10-year termination clause: if one side ends the agreement, it would have to pay towards rebuilding border-check infrastructure that the deal is expected to scale back. The published texts are also expected to explain how Britain will follow relevant EU rules without a vote and how ministers could use secondary legislation to align laws, with less parliamentary scrutiny.

content.headline: Poundland enters administration, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk
content.shortHeadline: Poundland collapses into administration with jobs at risk
content.standfirst: The retailer will keep trading while administrators seek a buyer for its 600 stores and distribution centres. The company’s failure to find a viable solvent deal puts jobs, suppliers and the chain’s future in doubt.

image.caption: A Poundland store. The retailer has entered administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.

sources.originalTitle: Poundland collapses, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk

segments.body: Poundland has entered administration after its owners rejected last-ditch bids to buy the business. Administrators say the sales process found no viable way to keep the company operating as a whole. Its 600 stores and distribution centres will remain open while they explore a sale of all or part of the business.

More than 10,000 jobs are at risk, and around 2,000 suppliers could lose business and payments for stock already delivered. The retailer’s owner, Gordon Brothers, says inflation and pressure on sales and margins left the business vulnerable. The Guardian reports that MPs have questioned payments and fees taken by the owner; the company has said it explored every avenue for a sale.

content.headline: England and Wales to create standalone stalking offence, ministers say
content.shortHeadline: New stalking offence will no longer require proof of fear
content.standfirst: The proposed law would focus on a perpetrator’s behaviour rather than requiring victims to prove fear or distress. A victims’ commissioner welcomes the change but says it does not address continued stalking after conviction.

image.caption: Alice Ruggles was murdered by an ex-partner who had stalked her.

sources.originalTitle: Ministers to create new stalking offence and scrap need for proof of fear or distress

segments.body: Ministers plan to make stalking a standalone offence in England and Wales, removing the requirement to establish harassment and prove a victim experienced fear or distress. The government also says courts can now directly impose stalking protection orders, even before an alleged perpetrator has been convicted.

The parents of Alice Ruggles, who was murdered by an ex-partner who stalked her, welcomed the proposal. Victims’ commissioner Claire Waxman called it welcome but an opportunity missed: she wants police to be able to arrest convicted stalkers who repeat their behaviour. The government says a new offence would be accompanied by stronger sentencing, with a maximum of 10 years in prison.

content.headline: Children in overcrowded homes are less likely to achieve good GCSEs, study finds
content.shortHeadline: Overcrowded homes linked to poorer GCSE results
content.standfirst: A study for the Sutton Trust links limited space and a lack of quiet places to study with weaker exam outcomes. Researchers urge a housing standard that gives children in rented homes room for a bedroom desk.

sources.originalTitle: Children in overcrowded homes get poorer GCSE results, study finds

segments.body: Research by University College London for the Sutton Trust found that children in poor housing conditions were less likely to achieve five good GCSEs or any A-levels. Young people without a suitable quiet place to study scored lower at 18, despite being level with peers at the end of primary school.

The researchers found that 52% of children in the poorest fifth of families shared a bedroom at age 11, compared with 7% in the richest fifth. The report calls for rented homes to meet a standard that provides space for a bedroom desk and suggests schools and councils offer more quiet study spaces. More than 170,000 children in England are in temporary accommodation, the report says.

content.headline: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
content.shortHeadline: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65
content.standfirst: Taylor co-wrote some of the band’s best-known songs and also worked with artists including Robert Palmer. His bandmates said he had been treated for prostate cancer and died at home on Monday.

image.caption: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor, who has died aged 65.

sources.originalTitle: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65

segments.body: Andy Taylor, guitarist with Duran Duran, has died aged 65 after a long battle with prostate cancer, the band said. Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote hits including “Rio”, “Save a Prayer” and “Girls on Film”, and later played on Robert Palmer’s “Addicted to Love”.

Taylor left Duran Duran in 1985, rejoined in 2000 and later departed again. He revealed in 2022 that he had stage-four metastatic prostate cancer, and contributed to the band’s 2023 album Danse Macabre. He is survived by his wife, children and grandson.

content.headline: Online influencers sell paid PIP claim advice as government plans clampdown
content.shortHeadline: Paid PIP claim advice faces government clampdown
content.standfirst: Some online advisers charge up to £99.99 for written responses to disability benefit forms. Experts warn there are no standard answers that secure an award, while the government says it plans a zero-fee cap for claims-management firms.

image.caption: An example of paid PIP claims advice posted online.

sources.originalTitle: The PIP influencers selling £100 packages of benefits tips

segments.body: Some online influencers and services charge disabled people for advice on claiming Personal Independence Payment (PIP), including packages offering written answers to copy into forms. The i Paper reports one provider charges £99.99 for a “done for you” package. The provider says its guidance is tailored to individual circumstances and does not submit claims.

Benefits experts warn against claims that particular words or standard answers can win PIP: assessors need detailed information about each claimant’s life and needs. TikTok adviser Noah Bear Nyle says misleading promises could exploit people’s uncertainty as reforms are considered. Minister Stephen Timms says the government plans a code of practice and a £0 fee cap for claims-management companies; how the wider PIP reforms will work remains unsettled.

content.headline: Parents say social media adds pressure to raising young children, survey finds
content.shortHeadline: Survey finds social media increases parenting anxiety
content.standfirst: In a poll of about 3,500 parents of children aged five and under, three-quarters said social media had increased their anxiety about parenting. Many also reported isolation and difficulty trusting advice.

sources.originalTitle: Social media making it harder for UK parents to raise families, survey finds

segments.body: A survey by early-years charity Kindred Squared found that 76% of participating parents of children aged five and under thought social media had increased anxiety around parenting. Three in five said they faced “impossible expectations” or felt judged, while 49% were concerned by conflicting online advice.

The survey also found that 12% of respondents had nobody outside their household they could call on in an emergency. Parents of children with special educational needs and disabilities were more likely to report difficulty accessing professional support. The findings are from about 3,500 parents and are a survey, not a measure of all families’ experiences.

content.headline: Denmark helps fund $622m package of equipment for Ukraine’s F-16s
content.shortHeadline: Denmark helps pay for Ukraine’s F-16 equipment
content.standfirst: The US has approved a $622m sale of maintenance equipment and other materiel for Ukraine’s F-16 aircraft. Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Norway will fund the transfer, with no US funds involved, according to the US State Department.

sources.originalTitle: Danmark med til at finansiere køb af amerikansk udstyr til Ukraine

segments.body: The US has approved the sale of $622m in maintenance equipment and other materiel for Ukraine’s F-16 fighter aircraft, according to the US State Department, cited by Ritzau. Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Norway will fund the purchase through the multinational Ukraine programme.

The State Department said no US money would be used for the transfer. The announcement identifies the funding partners and the approved value, but does not specify when the equipment will be delivered.

content.headline: Young people in Denmark, Greenland and Faroe Islands want closer ties, survey
content.shortHeadline: Young people back closer ties across the Danish realm
content.standfirst: A survey finds support for continued cooperation, alongside calls for greater mutual understanding. Awareness of Greenland has risen among young Danes during recent US attention, but knowledge of the Faroe Islands remains lower.

sources.originalTitle: Unge har fået øjnene op for Rigsfællesskabet. Men de kender stadig ikke hinanden særlig godt

segments.body: A report by Denmark’s Youth Council and partner organisations in Greenland and the Faroe Islands finds young people broadly support continued cooperation across the Danish realm, but want to know more about one another’s societies. DUF chair Anneline Larsen says closer cooperation requires greater equality between the countries.

Between 2024 and 2026, the share reporting high or very high knowledge rose by 27 percentage points among Faroese young people, 16 points among Greenlandic young people and four points among Danish young people. The report also found 69% of young Danes said recent attention had increased their knowledge of Greenland, compared with 30% who said the same about the Faroe Islands.

content.headline: EU leaders face budget deadlock over spending, Ukraine and new revenue
content.shortHeadline: EU budget talks face disputes over spending and new revenue
content.standfirst: EU leaders meet over the bloc’s next seven-year budget, with Denmark among those seeking a smaller plan and Germany pressing to include Ukraine support. Some lawmakers want new EU revenue, including a technology levy, but member states remain divided.

image.caption: German chancellor Friedrich Merz and French president Emmanuel Macron are pressing different demands in EU budget talks.

sources.originalTitle: Merz er på tværs og Macron kræver handling - svært EU-topmøde i vente
Kan en Elon Musk-skat hjælpe Europas økonomisk pressede politikere?

segments.body: EU leaders are meeting to discuss the next seven-year budget, with disputes over its size and priorities. Denmark and other northern European countries want the European Commission’s proposed budget cut by 10%. European Council president António Costa has put forward a smaller proposal, but it is unclear whether it can secure agreement.

perspectives.body: DR reports that many European Parliament members are arguing for new EU revenue, including a technology tax that could apply to large global companies, as well as levies on plastic and electronic waste. Member states are not united behind the proposals.

segments.body: Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz has demanded that support for Ukraine be included in the budget; Denmark’s prime minister supports that position. Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic oppose contributing to a new Ukraine package, according to political analyst Lykke Friis. France is also pressing for an agreement before the end of the year.

content.headline: South Greenland lifts alcohol sales ban but keeps limits on strong drinks
content.shortHeadline: South Greenland reopens alcohol sales with restrictions
content.standfirst: Kommune Kujalleq’s two-month ban on alcohol sales and service has ended after the municipal council’s decision was approved by Greenland’s government. Drinks stronger than 22.09% alcohol remain prohibited, and some residents oppose the reopening.

image.caption: A community in South Greenland, where alcohol sales have resumed under new restrictions.

sources.originalTitle: Sydgrønland åbner for alkohol igen - men med skærpede krav

segments.body: Alcohol sales and service have resumed in Greenland’s southernmost municipality, Kommune Kujalleq, after the municipal council voted to end a ban that began on 2 October. The ban followed serious alcohol-related incidents; Greenland’s government has approved the council’s decision.

The health ministry says drinks above 22.09% alcohol will remain prohibited. Police reports fell markedly during the ban, but restaurant owners and taxi drivers said they lost income. A demonstration in Qaqortoq focused on children’s welfare, and youth centres in several towns are due to stay open overnight as sales resume.

content.headline: Danish government partner criticises Frederiksen’s use of ‘population exchange’
content.shortHeadline: Government partner challenges Frederiksen over migration phrase
content.standfirst: Moderates’ political spokesperson Mohammad Rona says the term has far-right associations and risks making Danish citizens with immigrant backgrounds feel suspected. The phrase has also been praised by far-right figures elsewhere in Europe.

image.caption: Moderates’ political spokesperson Mohammad Rona has criticised the prime minister’s choice of words.

sources.originalTitle: Politisk ordfører: Selvfølgelig rammer omstridt højrefløjsord også 'personligt'
Mens Mette Frederiksen-udtalelse skaber problemer herhjemme, bliver den hyldet andre steder

segments.body: Mohammad Rona, the Moderates’ political spokesperson, has criticised Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen for saying she opposed a large “population exchange”. Rona says the term is associated with a far-right conspiracy theory and is a dangerous choice of words, even though he supports debate about Denmark’s immigration policy.

Rona says the wording affected him personally and raised concerns for people with immigrant backgrounds, including his Afghan-born parents. DR reports that far-right figures in Germany, Austria and France praised Frederiksen’s remarks and urged others to spread them. Frederiksen has rejected being associated with conspiracy theorists or far-right movements.

perspectives.body: DR’s reporting from Europe shows the phrase resonated with far-right politicians and activists abroad, while a Le Monde correspondent said even French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has avoided using it.

content.headline: EU court orders Commission to set timetable for ending farm animal cages
content.shortHeadline: EU court orders timetable for ending farm animal cages
content.standfirst: The European Commission must say when it intends to propose a ban after failing to deliver on a 2021 promise. The court’s ruling does not itself prohibit cages; about 300 million farm animals are held in them across the EU, the report says.

image.caption: Farm animals in cages; the EU court has ordered the Commission to set out a timetable for a proposed ban.

sources.originalTitle: EU-Domstolen vil have plan for forbud mod landbrugsdyr i bur

segments.body: The EU Court of Justice has ordered the European Commission to set out when it intends to introduce a proposal to end the use of cages for farm animals. The Commission promised a legislative proposal in 2021 but did not deliver one or provide a new timetable, prompting campaigners to take legal action.

The case followed a citizens’ initiative backed by almost 1.4 million signatures. The ruling requires the Commission to state its plans; it does not itself ban cages. Animal welfare group Dyrenes Beskyttelse called the decision a historic victory, while the farming sector has previously warned that a ban could increase costs for consumers.

content.headline: More Germans are moving to Southern Denmark, regional figures show
content.shortHeadline: German residents in Southern Denmark rise 48% since 2022
content.standfirst: New figures show 1,335 German citizens moved to the Region of Southern Denmark in the second half of 2025 and first half of 2026. The rise is strongest in the four southern Jutland municipalities, while cross-border commuting has declined.

sources.originalTitle: Markant udvikling i antallet af tyskere i Sønderjylland

segments.body: The number of German citizens living in the Region of Southern Denmark has risen 48% since 2022, reaching 14,440, according to an annual report on Danish-German cooperation. A total of 1,335 Germans moved to the region in the second half of 2025 and first half of 2026; the largest increases were in Haderslev, Sønderborg, Aabenraa and Tønder.

Tønder’s German population has more than doubled since 2018, while the number of people living in Germany and commuting to work in Denmark fell 13.5% between 2022 and 2024. A 2023 survey of German residents in Aabenraa and Sønderborg cited affordable housing, safety, nature and Danish culture among reasons for moving; work was not the main factor.

content.headline: Danes’ average net worth reaches record, but wealth remains uneven
content.shortHeadline: Danish net worth hits record as wealth gaps persist
content.standfirst: Statistics Denmark puts average net wealth at DKK 2.362m in 2025, with rising house prices a major factor. The median is lower and varies sharply by age, gender and municipality, while the wealthiest quarter has gained more since 2020.

sources.originalTitle: Se listen – er du lige så rig som andre på din alder?

segments.body: The average net wealth of Danish residents reached DKK 2.362m in 2025, up 6.6% on the previous year, according to Statistics Denmark. Median net wealth—the midpoint, with half of people above and half below—was DKK 887,000. Rising house prices helped lift the figures.

Wealth differed substantially by age and gender: median net wealth was DKK 2.4m for people aged 65 to 69, compared with DKK 123,000 for those aged 25 to 29; the median was DKK 1.015m for men and DKK 789,000 for women. The top quarter’s wealth rose more than the bottom quarter’s between 2020 and 2025.

content.headline: Pochettino’s Manchester United held in chaotic 2-2 draw at Sporting
content.shortHeadline: United held 2-2 by Sporting amid Lisbon chaos
content.standfirst: Manchester United twice took the lead in a game shaped by penalties, goalkeeping errors and disputed decisions. Mauricio Pochettino is still waiting for his first win after two matches in charge.

image.caption: Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino during the 2-2 draw with Sporting.

sources.originalTitle: Frustration reigns for Pochettino in chaotic start to Man Utd job
Divots, howlers and bad decisions - dissecting Man Utd's draw in Lisbon

segments.body: Manchester United drew 2-2 with Sporting in Lisbon, leaving Mauricio Pochettino without a win in his first two games as head coach. United fell behind after Senne Lammens gave away a penalty, then levelled through Bruno Fernandes from the spot and went ahead when Fernandes’ shot took an unexpected bounce off a divot.

segments.title: A night of disputed decisions
segments.body: Lammens later dropped the ball for Sporting’s equaliser, and United had a potential late winner ruled out after a VAR review. Referee Szymon Marciniak also disallowed Amad’s first-half goal after blowing for a foul before the ball crossed the line. Ashley Young called that decision a disgrace; BBC Sport’s Dale Johnson explained that, once the whistle had gone, VAR could not review the goal.

content.headline: Isak scores twice as Liverpool beat Club Brugge to return to winning ways
content.shortHeadline: Isak double helps Liverpool beat Club Brugge
content.standfirst: Alexander Isak’s two goals took his season tally to 10 as Liverpool won 3-0 in Belgium. The striker has scored four times in his past four games after an injury-disrupted start at the club.

sources.originalTitle: 'All coming together' - Isak repaying Liverpool faith

segments.body: Alexander Isak scored twice in Liverpool’s 3-0 Champions League win over Club Brugge, taking his total for the season to 10. He has scored four goals in his past four matches and has now found the net in six consecutive away games.

segments.title: More than goals
segments.body: Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola praised Isak’s link-up play as well as his finishing, while former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock said the striker looked fitter and sharper. Florian Wirtz also continued a strong run, with eight goal contributions in his past five games for Liverpool and Germany, according to the report.

content.headline: England make five changes for Saturday’s All Blacks rematch
content.shortHeadline: Fisilau to make first England start against New Zealand
content.standfirst: Greg Fisilau will make his first England start as Steve Borthwick names five changes for Saturday’s rematch with New Zealand. A win would give England an autumn clean sweep and six victories in a row.

image.caption: Greg Fisilau has impressed as a replacement for England in recent weeks.

sources.originalTitle: Fisilau starts as England change five for All Blacks rematch

segments.body: Exeter back-row Greg Fisilau has been named in England’s starting XV for the first time, one of five changes for Saturday’s match against New Zealand. Freddie Steward, Tommy Freeman, Ellis Genge and Luke Cowan-Dickie also come into the starting side.

segments.title: A chance to make an impression
segments.body: Fisilau has impressed as a replacement in England’s previous three autumn wins. Borthwick said he wanted to see the 23-year-old bring his carrying power and work-rate from the start. England can secure an autumn clean sweep, a sixth consecutive win and third place in the Nations Championship standings with victory.

content.headline: Raheem Sterling receives suspended 12-month sentence for dangerous driving
content.shortHeadline: Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving
content.standfirst: The former England and Premier League forward was given a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, and disqualified from driving for two years. His playing career has stalled since leaving Chelsea.

sources.originalTitle: Raheem Sterling - from national icon to suspended jail sentence

segments.body: Raheem Sterling has received a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. He was also disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to complete 100 hours of unpaid work. At an earlier hearing, Sterling admitted dangerous driving after a motorway crash in May.

segments.title: A career at a crossroads
segments.body: Sterling, 31, scored 20 goals in 82 England appearances and won four Premier League titles. He has not played since appearing for Feyenoord in May, following a short-term move there after a difficult spell at Chelsea and an unsuccessful loan at Arsenal.

content.headline: Football regulator says it will act if Manchester City ruling is upheld
content.shortHeadline: Regulator vows action if Man City ruling stands
content.standfirst: Independent Football Regulator chair David Kogan told MPs the watchdog would not avoid its duties because of Manchester City’s size. Any action would depend on the outcome of the club’s appeal and the evidence against individuals.

sources.originalTitle: Regulator chief 'has stomach' to face Man City

segments.body: The chair of English football’s Independent Football Regulator, David Kogan, told MPs it would take appropriate action if the circumstances required it, regardless of a club’s size. Manchester City deny wrongdoing and have appealed an independent commission’s finding that they breached Premier League financial rules over nine seasons.

segments.title: What action could follow?
segments.body: If the ruling is upheld, the regulator could investigate City’s hierarchy. Its powers include removing directors deemed unsuitable and, in the most serious case, forcing a sale of the club. The regulator’s chair said the evidence and any appeal judgment would be central to its decision.

content.headline: O’Sullivan loses to 61-year-old Drago as poor form continues
content.shortHeadline: Drago beats O’Sullivan as snooker struggles continue
content.standfirst: Ronnie O’Sullivan lost 5-3 to former professional Tony Drago at the Snooker 900 event in Reading. The seven-time world champion had won his opening match but has struggled in recent tournaments.

sources.originalTitle: O'Sullivan continues poor form with Drago loss

segments.body: Ronnie O’Sullivan’s difficult run continued with a 5-3 defeat by 61-year-old Tony Drago at the Snooker 900 tournament in Reading. O’Sullivan had beaten Barry Pinches in his opening match, but has also recently lost in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open and 4-0 to Shaun Murphy at the Champion of Champions.

segments.title: Qualification concerns
segments.body: O’Sullivan last won a ranking event at the World Grand Prix in January 2024. The report says he is in danger of slipping out of the automatic qualifying places for the 2028 World Championship, although he should reach the 2027 event. World champion Wu Yize and reigning champion Neil Robertson were also eliminated from the tournament.

content.headline: Dottin timed out at the crease, but Renegades win WBBL thriller
content.shortHeadline: Dottin timed out as Renegades complete WBBL chase
content.standfirst: Deandra Dottin was dismissed without facing a ball after umpires ruled she had taken too long to get ready. Melbourne Renegades still chased down Brisbane Heat’s 138 on the final delivery to win by three wickets.

image.caption: Sarah Glenn’s delivery to the empty stumps dismissed Deandra Dottin for a golden duck.

sources.originalTitle: Dottin out to 'free ball' after historic WBBL decision

segments.body: Melbourne Renegades batter Deandra Dottin was timed out in an unusual Women’s Big Bash League dismissal after taking longer than the 75-second limit to prepare to face. Sarah Glenn bowled at the empty stumps and hit them, removing Dottin for a golden duck.

segments.title: A dramatic finish
segments.body: The wicket left the Renegades at 97-5, still needing 41 from 34 balls. They recovered to complete their chase of Brisbane Heat’s 138 on the final delivery, winning by three wickets.

content.headline: Fans pay tribute to Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel after his death
content.shortHeadline: Fans pay tribute to Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel
content.standfirst: Supporters gathered to remember Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel, who died after suffering a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match. The supplied report does not give further details about the incident.

sources.originalTitle: Fans pay respects to Tenerife's De Miguel

segments.body: Fans gathered to pay their respects to Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel after his death. The supplied report says he suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match but does not provide further details about the incident.

content.headline: Beatles’ Savile Row rooftop site approved as visitor attraction
content.shortHeadline: Beatles’ Savile Row site approved, but no rooftop gigs
content.standfirst: A seven-storey exhibition and cultural attraction is planned for the building where the Beatles were based and played their final public show. The approval comes with a ban on live music on the rooftop.

image.caption: The Beatles performing on the rooftop of 3 Savile Row in 1969.

sources.originalTitle: Beatles attraction at 3 Savile Row approved – with ban on rooftop gigs

segments.body: Westminster council has unanimously approved plans to turn 3 Savile Row, the Beatles’ former headquarters and the site of their 1969 rooftop performance, into a seven-storey exhibition and cultural attraction. Apple Corps has said it hopes to open the venue in 2027.

segments.title: A rooftop without live music
segments.body: Visitors will be able to access the roof, but live music is prohibited. Amplified music will be allowed at controlled noise levels. The plans also include a cafe-bar, a replica studio and an exhibition shop; a booking system is intended to prevent queues.

The Savile Row Bespoke Association raised concerns about congestion on the street’s narrow pavements and the effect of visitor numbers on local businesses. Apple Corps estimates the attraction could draw up to 900 people a day on weekdays and 1,140 at weekends.

content.headline: Peter Gabriel on a new album, AI and the ideas that keep derailing him
content.shortHeadline: Peter Gabriel on AI, music and the joy of getting sidetracked
content.standfirst: The musician’s 13-track, 90-minute album arrives with two mixes, but an interview ranges from creativity and artificial intelligence to consciousness and animal communication. His digressions, he says, feed the work.

image.caption: Peter Gabriel, whose interests range from music to artificial intelligence and animal communication.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel

segments.body: Peter Gabriel’s new album, o\i, runs nearly 90 minutes and will be released in two versions: a “dark” mix by Tchad Blake and a “bright” one by Mark “Spike” Stent. Gabriel describes the long songs as an extension of his interest in African music and his willingness, at 76, to make what he wants.

segments.title: A creative mind in motion
segments.body: An interview about the record wanders through Gabriel’s interests in consciousness, communication with other species and scientific research. He sees his diversions as part of his creative process: conversations and ideas outside the album cycle, he argues, can enrich the music.

segments.title: Tools and risks
segments.body: Gabriel is enthusiastic about AI as a creative tool, but says its use in warfare is frightening and calls for international agreements, safeguards and a means of control. He also speculates about people becoming more closely integrated with AI; these are his views, not settled predictions.

content.headline: Life Without Buildings reunite after their music finds a new audience
content.shortHeadline: Life Without Buildings return after a TikTok-fuelled rediscovery
content.standfirst: The Glasgow band split in 2002 after a brief, obscure run. A Frank Ocean play and a viral TikTok helped new listeners find their idiosyncratic music, but the returning group worried that reunion gigs might diminish what they had left behind.

image.caption: Life Without Buildings pictured around the release of their debut album.

sources.originalTitle: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?

segments.body: Life Without Buildings played their first proper gig together in almost 25 years at Glasgow’s Mono. The band, whose brief career produced one album, Any Other City, and a handful of singles, are back for four shows linked to Rough Trade’s 50th-anniversary celebrations.

segments.title: An unexpected second life
segments.body: The group’s rediscovery gathered pace after Frank Ocean played “The Leanover” on his Apple Music show in 2018. Later, a TikTok video of Beabadoobee miming to the song’s opening seconds helped it travel further. Singer Sue Tompkins’ spoken, rhythmic vocals remain central to the band’s singular sound.

The musicians say they had been wary of returning, concerned that new attention might spoil their memory of a joyful but commercially difficult time. Their first reunion performance brought the old songs back to life, Tompkins said, and left her energised by playing with her bandmates again.

content.headline: Judee Sill’s music finds new listeners decades after her death
content.shortHeadline: Judee Sill’s overlooked songs are finding new listeners
content.standfirst: The singer-songwriter’s intricate folk and gospel music once drew critical acclaim, but her career faded and she died aged 35. Covers by later artists and a documentary are bringing renewed attention to a catalogue that still feels precarious.

image.caption: Judee Sill in London in 1972, as her music career was beginning to rise.

sources.originalTitle: The forgotten folk genius who’s finally getting her due after dying in obscurity

segments.body: Judee Sill’s two albums combined folk, country and gospel with complex arrangements and devotional songwriting. Signed to David Geffen’s Asylum Records, she was once presented as a rising star, but her second album, Heart Food, did not sell well and she was dropped from the label.

segments.title: A difficult life, a lasting body of work
segments.body: Sill faced addiction, homelessness, prison, violence and chronic pain. She died in 1979 at 35. The account notes uncertainty about the circumstances of her death: it was ruled a suicide, although some believe the note found nearby was a plea for help rather than a suicide note.

Her songs have been covered by artists including Fleet Foxes, Weyes Blood and Big Thief. The documentary Lost Angel and the release of her final recordings have also helped introduce her work to new listeners, though the piece argues that her place in the wider musical canon remains fragile.

content.headline: Weird Baile’s internet-born Brazilian funk gets an archival release
content.shortHeadline: Weird Baile’s lost Brazilian funk finds an official release
content.standfirst: TraTraTrax has assembled tracks made over two decades by an online collective working on the fringes of Brazilian funk. The review hears an influential, carefully sequenced archive, though its dark minimalism leaves some of the group’s playful side behind.

sources.originalTitle: Collected Rips 2004-2024

segments.body: Collected Rips 2004-2024 brings together 14 previously unreleased tracks by Weird Baile, an internet-based group of Brazilian producers and DJs. The label says the recordings were assembled from MP3 rips, voice notes and lost project files, preserving music that helped shape an online strand of funk.

segments.title: A scene without a single home
segments.body: The review describes the collective as rooted in the internet rather than a particular city or baile. Its tracks draw on different regional forms of Brazilian funk and outside references, from Migos samples to UK bass, creating a sound shaped by online circulation as much as by local scenes.

The compilation’s dark, sparse beats make for a coherent listen, and the closing track brings a more playful, loose energy. The reviewer’s reservation is that the selection could have included more of the fun that made Weird Baile intriguing in the first place.

content.headline: Thoom fuses Arabic instrumentation and hyperpop on a vivid debut
content.shortHeadline: Thoom turns hyperpop into a vivid, personal debut
content.standfirst: The Beirut-raised, Los Angeles-based artist brings oud and other Arabic sounds into abrasive club pop, making space for both theatrical excess and vulnerable songwriting. The record’s closing song turns toward Lebanon and the uncertainty of return.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, Thoom—artist Zeynab Marwan—joins hyperpop production with Arabic instrumentation. The review describes a sound that moves between pounding club tracks, pop drama and quieter, more ominous songs, with Marwan’s voice able to shift from melodic warmth to menace.

segments.title: Intensity with feeling
segments.body: The review hears the strongest work in songs where volatile production deepens the emotional material rather than overwhelming it. “Morocco” turns a lover’s cruelty into a restrained threat, while the fierce “On the Floor” puts Marwan’s voice against relentless drums and sharp synths.

Closer “I’m Going Back to Lebanon” links longing for home with uncertainty about the country’s future. The reviewer calls it the clearest expression of the album’s stakes, while finding some of the more conventional pop moments less distinctive.

content.headline: Armand Hammer’s new album turns everyday scenes into political writing
content.shortHeadline: Armand Hammer turn daily life into urgent political rap
content.standfirst: On Snakes & Ladders, billy woods and Elucid bring together a wide circle of independent producers for fractured, searching rap. The review hears a record that connects personal observation with the pressures of race, power and political anxiety.

sources.originalTitle: Snakes & Ladders

segments.body: Snakes & Ladders, surprise-released by Backwoodz Studioz, is a new album from New York duo Armand Hammer. Across dense, fragmented verses, billy woods and Elucid draw meaning from ordinary settings—a street walk, a job application—and connect those moments to broader histories of power and displacement.

segments.title: A collective sound
segments.body: The production comes from a broad roster of collaborators, including clipping., Preservation, Kenny Segal and Child Actor. Despite the range of contributors, the review finds a shared atmosphere: unsettling, varied beats that give the rappers room to move between sharply different writing and vocal styles.

The review frames the album’s political weight as an alternative measure of rap’s cultural value, beyond commercial success. It describes the record as demanding rather than easy listening, with its anxieties and histories deliberately left unresolved.

content.headline: Font’s American Bully XL brings country ache into industrial noise
content.shortHeadline: Font bring country heartbreak into noisy, confessional songs
content.standfirst: The Texas band’s second album trades some of its debut’s obscurity for more exposed songwriting. Its warped country references and abrasive production make the vulnerability feel less like a change of style than a new source of tension.

sources.originalTitle: American Bully XL

segments.body: On American Bully XL, Font move toward more direct, confessional lyrics while keeping the industrial distortion and restless arrangements of their earlier work. The review hears songs about heartbreak and the desire for recognition, delivered through a crowded mix of synths, sampling, guitars and percussion.

segments.title: Tenderness through distortion
segments.body: The album’s country influence appears in fragments: fingerpicking, wavering keyboard lines and ballad-like melodies, often blurred by harsh production. On “Texas,” the sounds shift between something like lap steel and a dial tone as the narrator pleads for a relationship to return.

content.headline: 14th review: Ava DuVernay makes a forceful case for the US Constitution
content.shortHeadline: Ava DuVernay’s 14th defends constitutional rights
content.standfirst: In her follow-up to 13th, DuVernay turns to the 14th Amendment and the rights it established. The review praises the documentary’s historical argument and its urgent defence of those protections against contemporary threats.

image.caption: Ava DuVernay in her documentary 14th.

sources.originalTitle: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants

segments.body: Ava DuVernay’s 14th examines the constitutional amendment that established birthright citizenship, due process and equal protection under the law. The film also considers the amendment’s bar on insurrectionists holding public office, arguing that these provisions are under threat.

segments.title: History and the present
segments.body: The review highlights the film’s account of the Reconstruction amendments after the American Civil War, and the backlash that followed. DuVernay draws a parallel between that history and what the reviewer describes as a contemporary reaction to Barack Obama’s presidency.

content.headline: Why Hollywood keeps returning to its imagined golden age
content.shortHeadline: Hollywood’s nostalgia boom meets an industry in crisis
content.standfirst: A new Cliff Booth film joins a wave of stories looking back at old Los Angeles. The feature argues that the appeal of that Hollywood past is inseparable from the present-day film industry’s job losses, shrinking production and fears about AI.

image.caption: Quentin Tarantino with Leonardo DiCaprio and Brad Pitt during the making of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.

sources.originalTitle: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories

segments.body: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is part of a recent run of films revisiting Los Angeles and Hollywood’s past, alongside works by Paul Thomas Anderson, Damien Chazelle and Ti West. These films look back to the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s through the stories and atmosphere of an earlier city.

segments.title: Nostalgia in a changing industry
segments.body: The feature links this revival to a present marked by declining local production, post-pandemic box-office pressures and significant job losses. It also notes the anxiety that AI could further hollow out film work and the city’s creative infrastructure.

The piece questions whether the films are recovering an authentic golden age or reproducing Hollywood’s longstanding talent for fabrication. It points to Los Angeles Plays Itself as a more sceptical account of a city built on constant reinvention.

content.headline: Jane Alexander looks back on five decades of acting and arts advocacy
content.shortHeadline: Jane Alexander on a career shaped by theatre and public service
content.standfirst: The actor recalls her breakthrough in The Great White Hope, a career spanning film and theatre, and her time leading the US National Endowment for the Arts. She also discusses harassment in the industry and the struggle to keep public arts funding available.

image.caption: Jane Alexander, who says she is glad the #MeToo movement brought harassment into the open.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom

segments.body: Jane Alexander’s performance in The Great White Hope brought her a Tony Award, a husband and her first film role. The play, about boxer Jack Johnson and an interracial marriage in segregated America, also brought her hate mail and death threats. Alexander remembers Muhammad Ali seeing his own story in the production.

segments.title: Work, power and the arts
segments.body: Alexander says the casting couch was an overt part of the industry: she turned down advances, while recognising that other actresses faced different choices and vulnerabilities. She welcomes the #MeToo movement. Later, as chair of the National Endowment for the Arts, she travelled widely to argue that access to art should extend beyond major cities.

She warns that cuts to arts funding threaten access for audiences and support for complex work, while noting that theatre prices already limit who can attend. At 87, Alexander says she has no plans to retire and remains committed to both art and nature.

content.headline: Josephine turns a director’s childhood trauma into a difficult film
content.shortHeadline: Josephine asks what a child carries after witnessing rape
content.standfirst: Beth de Araújo’s drama draws on an assault she witnessed as a child and follows an eight-year-old struggling to understand what she saw. The film’s graphic opening and its approach to young performers raise difficult questions about depicting sexual violence.

image.caption: Beth de Araújo with Channing Tatum, Mason Reeves and Gemma Chan.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine

segments.body: Writer-director Beth de Araújo says she drew on her own childhood experience for Josephine. In the film, an eight-year-old witnesses a rape and begins to interpret the world around her through fear. The story follows her confusion and her parents’ attempts to help, which do not immediately address what she needs to know.

segments.title: A deliberate choice
segments.body: The film shows the assault Josephine witnesses in graphic detail. De Araújo argues that the audience needs to see what the child sees to understand the fear shaping the rest of the story. The child actor, Mason Reeves, was not present for the assault scene and did not read the script.

The feature also describes how the film draws on de Araújo’s work as a witness advocate and on research into sexual-assault cases. She says she does not regard trauma as something that is simply resolved, and that the film’s release has nevertheless coincided with her being able to sleep through the night.

content.headline: Way of the Warrior Kid review: Chris Pratt’s film turns bullying into boot camp
content.shortHeadline: Way of the Warrior Kid treats bullying with military drills
content.standfirst: The review faults this family film for answering a bullied boy’s problems with physical training and cage-fighting. It argues that the story’s easy celebration of machismo misses the chance to treat its young characters and their family circumstances with more care.

image.caption: Chris Pratt and Jude Hill in Way of the Warrior Kid.

sources.originalTitle: Way of the Warrior Kid review - Chris Pratt’s family film is as subtle as a military recruitment video

segments.body: In Way of the Warrior Kid, a bullied 13-year-old is put through a strict training plan by his Navy SEAL uncle. The routine includes exercise, chores and a summer job, but also cage-fighting—an escalation the review sees as an implausible response to the boy’s troubles.

segments.title: A missed opportunity
segments.body: The reviewer finds the film’s treatment of the boy’s widowed mother especially ungenerous, and says any suggestions that the uncle is carrying trauma from combat are quickly brushed aside. The third act offers some excitement, but does not undo the film’s broader reliance on machismo and military imagery.

content.headline: The Slightest Touch follows Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s friendship
content.shortHeadline: Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s friendship on screen
content.standfirst: Rachel Fleit’s documentary follows Farrell and Fogarty as they prepare for the Dublin Marathon, with Farrell set to push her wheelchair for the final miles. The review finds a warm friendship story that also allows space for Farrell’s grief and family life.

image.caption: Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty in The Slightest Touch.

sources.originalTitle: The Slightest Touch review – running marathons in Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s odd-couple friendship

segments.body: Emma Fogarty, an advocate for people with epidermolysis bullosa, has a long friendship with Colin Farrell, who supports the Irish charity Debra. The documentary follows them preparing for the 2025 Dublin Marathon, where Farrell runs and pushes Fogarty in her modified wheelchair for the final two miles.

segments.title: More than a race
segments.body: The film also shows Farrell speaking about his father’s final weeks and his eldest son, who has Angelman syndrome. The reviewer describes him as emotionally open while noting that the documentary keeps much of the pair’s private lives carefully controlled.

content.headline: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth brings Brad Pitt back to 1977 LA
content.shortHeadline: Brad Pitt returns as Cliff Booth in a 1970s LA caper
content.standfirst: David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s continuation of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, with Pitt’s stuntman turned fixer at its centre. The review enjoys the film’s energy and comic style while noting that it leaves key questions and much of its story unresolved.

image.caption: Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

sources.originalTitle: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review – Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return

segments.body: Set in Los Angeles in 1977, the film follows Cliff Booth after he has left stunt work and taken on a collection of side jobs, including discreetly helping people in the film industry who are being extorted. Elizabeth Debicki’s talent agent brings him into a new criminal entanglement.

segments.title: Pitt’s easygoing centre
segments.body: The review praises Brad Pitt’s imperturbable performance, which gives the film its comic charge, and describes Fincher’s direction as brisker than Tarantino’s chapter-driven style. It also notes how the film leaves the question of Cliff’s wife largely untouched.

content.headline: You Can See Everything blurs Nathan Fielder’s documentary and its subject
content.shortHeadline: A documentary turns Elizabeth Holmes into an uneasy puzzle
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder’s film follows Elizabeth Holmes and her family before her prison sentence, raising questions about truth, sympathy and control over a public image. The review is captivated by the experiment but uneasy about how its subject’s story is reframed.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: Elizabeth Holmes is not the villain of You Can See Everything. That’s a problem

segments.body: You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes in the month before she reports to prison for her Theranos fraud conviction. Holmes and her husband invited a film crew into their home, seeking to tell a more personal story after years of public scrutiny.

segments.title: Who controls the story?
segments.body: Director Nathan Fielder is known for work that blurs documentary and performance. The review describes him watching Holmes closely while questioning whether she is sincere, manipulative or both—an uncertainty that grows as he becomes more involved in her life.

The review finds the film’s second half changes focus toward Holmes’s husband, whose behaviour and use of an AI model of her complicate the story further. It argues that this shift risks making Holmes seem more sympathetic, while leaving unresolved how much of what the audience sees is performance.

content.headline: Blade Runner 2099 review: a neon-lit vision of a world turned upside down
content.shortHeadline: Blade Runner 2099 is a haunting TV expansion of the films
content.standfirst: Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer lead the franchise’s first television story, set decades after Blade Runner 2049. The review praises its haunting visual world and mood, while wishing it made more room for episodic storytelling.

image.caption: A neon-lit scene from Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty

segments.body: In Blade Runner 2099, replicants have become blade runners, hunting disobedient humans. Michelle Yeoh plays Olwen, an ageing replicant, and Hunter Schafer plays Cora, a human impersonating one. Their search for a former colleague becomes a story about memory and identity.

segments.title: Atmosphere over explanation
segments.body: The review values the series’ images and mood over a fully explained world: neon, shadow, abandoned spaces and a soundtrack of synths and saxophone. It also finds sharp visual unease in details such as the devices used to restrain people and the places where replicants imitate human life.

The series brings the franchise’s questions about memory into an era of anxiety about machine-made images and text. The reviewer finds its doomsday visions memorable, though argues that a clearer episodic structure might have strengthened the story.

content.headline: Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure finds joy in friendship and memory
content.shortHeadline: Prue and Sandi’s South African trip is a joyful travelogue
content.standfirst: Prue Leith revisits places she knew growing up in South Africa, accompanied by Sandi Toksvig. The review celebrates their easy friendship while also highlighting Leith’s reflections on apartheid and the country’s changing present.

image.caption: Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig in Simon’s Town, South Africa.

sources.originalTitle: Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure review – you’ll feel lucky to have this joyful show in your life

segments.body: The six-part series follows Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig around South Africa. Leith, who left the country for England at 20, revisits places from her childhood, while Toksvig’s lively curiosity turns the trip into an affectionate two-hander.

segments.title: Memory and history
segments.body: In Cape Town, Leith remembers the city of her youth and speaks with a woman whose family was forcibly moved during apartheid. Leith says she was raised to oppose apartheid but feels ashamed that she was not more conscious of everyday injustices as a teenager.

The review finds the series’ warmth in the pair’s friendship and their willingness to reflect as well as enjoy the journey. Leith says she wanted to make the programme while she and Toksvig were still able to travel together.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson gives The Great British Bake Off a fresh flavour
content.shortHeadline: Nigella Lawson brings new energy to Bake Off
content.standfirst: The review credits Lawson’s vivid food commentary, warmth and camp humour with helping revive the baking competition. It also points to strong viewing figures and format changes as signs that the show’s latest series has connected with audiences.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson with fellow Bake Off judge Paul Hollywood.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The icing on the cake’: how Nigella saved Bake Off

segments.body: Nigella Lawson has replaced Prue Leith as a judge on The Great British Bake Off, alongside Paul Hollywood. The review says Lawson’s enthusiastic attention to flavour and gift for description have made her a distinctive presence in the tent.

segments.title: A change in the mix
segments.body: The programme has added new formats, including an Audience Choice week and challenges based on illustrations rather than recipes. The article reports that the first episode drew 7.1 million viewers, ahead of Strictly Come Dancing’s launch episode, and says Channel 4 has signed Lawson for another series.

content.headline: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle makes history a lively tour
content.shortHeadline: Lucy Worsley unlocks the history behind Europe’s castles
content.standfirst: Worsley’s four-part series explores the Doge’s Palace, Versailles, Blenheim and Neuschwanstein. The review praises her accessible approach and the programme’s ability to connect grand buildings with the power, politics and people behind them.

image.caption: Lucy Worsley exploring Venice’s Doge’s Palace.

sources.originalTitle: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle review – heavenly TV that instantly brightens up your day

segments.body: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle begins at Venice’s Doge’s Palace and continues to Versailles, Blenheim and Neuschwanstein. The review praises Worsley for inviting other historians into the story and making complex history easy to follow.

segments.title: The stories inside the walls
segments.body: The series presents the Doge’s Palace as a centre of government and surveillance, not simply a grand residence. It also explores the prison below it, the escape of Casanova, Venice’s changing fortunes and the building’s later transformation into a tourist destination.

At Versailles and Blenheim, the programme turns to monarchy, family life and the architecture of power. Its final stop is Ludwig II’s Neuschwanstein, a castle shaped by Romanticism and Wagner, whose builder’s death in a nearby lake remains unexplained.

content.headline: The Witch Farm turns Danny Robins’s paranormal podcast into drama
content.shortHeadline: The Witch Farm brings a real-life haunting to TV
content.standfirst: Robins’s drama adapts his podcast account of a family’s unsettling experiences in the Welsh countryside. He says the story leaves room for uncertainty, rather than claiming to prove that ghosts are real.

image.caption: Danny Robins, creator of The Witch Farm and host of the Uncanny podcast.

sources.originalTitle: Danny Robins: ‘My wife has never listened to Uncanny. She finds it terrifying’

segments.body: The Witch Farm is a four-part BBC drama inspired by accounts of a family’s experiences at a remote Welsh farmhouse between 1989 and 1996. Its story follows Bill, his pregnant partner Liz and his teenage son as unsettling events make them question whether they are alone.

segments.title: Holding space for doubt
segments.body: Danny Robins, whose podcast investigated the case, says he does not consider himself a believer. He describes his approach as one that takes people’s accounts seriously without turning them into proof of the supernatural, including when witnesses may be dealing with difficult personal circumstances.

Robins traces his interest in the unexplained to childhood, when ghost stories left room for uncertainty. He thinks today’s children are more often given fully explained fictional worlds, though he acknowledges that the question of what lies beyond death is partly personal.

content.headline: Russell Brand documentary Open Secret examines an industry’s complicity
content.shortHeadline: Open Secret examines how Russell Brand’s behaviour was enabled
content.standfirst: The documentary combines testimony from people in Brand’s orbit with footage of his public persona and the reporting that led to his conviction. The review argues that its most disturbing point is how often his behaviour was visible and excused.

image.caption: Russell Brand in the Netflix documentary Open Secret.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Russell Brand documentary feels like a horror film

segments.body: Open Secret follows the reporting by Sunday Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace and includes interviews with comedians, writers and former partners. The review notes that Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault and has begun serving a prison sentence.

segments.title: What was allowed in public
segments.body: The reviewer says the film’s force comes from setting accounts of harm alongside footage of Brand’s celebrity years, when sexualised jokes and boundary-crossing behaviour were often treated as part of his public image. Some testimony is attributed to women describing alleged abuse; the article distinguishes those accounts from the convictions.

The review argues that Brand’s conduct was enabled by a wider culture that valued the “bad boy” persona and left people who wanted to speak out fearing they would not be believed. It sees the documentary’s central indictment as extending beyond one individual to the institutions and audiences that tolerated him.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future follows years of creative and commercial strain
content.shortHeadline: What went wrong for Doctor Who—and what could bring it back?
content.standfirst: The BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special and ended its partnership with Disney+, leaving the long-running series without a current Doctor or confirmed next step. Fans and writers differ on whether it needs a pause, new backing or simply a return to television.

image.caption: Illustrations of several actors who have played Doctor Who.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since its 2025 series, starring Ncuti Gatwa, and the BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special. The broadcaster has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and is seeking a new partner to help fund future production, but none has yet been announced.

segments.title: A series built to change
segments.body: The feature traces the programme’s revivals and repeated changes of lead actor and showrunner. Some fans argue the latest scripts became harder to follow; others point to the show’s long tradition of reinvention as a reason it can return.

Comedian Frank Skinner says he does not understand why the BBC has kept the show off air for so long, while writer Mark Gatiss has suggested a break may be appropriate. No decision on a new Doctor or production partner is reported.

content.headline: I’m a Celebrity row over AJ Odudu’s ‘aggressive’ label prompts debate
content.shortHeadline: An I’m a Celebrity exchange reignites debate over stereotyping
content.standfirst: A reviewer argues that Mariella Frostrup’s description of AJ Odudu as “aggressive” echoed a familiar stereotype about Black women. The article reports that fellow campmates disagreed with Frostrup’s reading of the exchange.

image.caption: AJ Odudu in I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here!

sources.originalTitle: Mariella Frostrup’s behaviour is all too familiar to Black women like me

segments.body: On I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here!, AJ Odudu challenged Mariella Frostrup after Frostrup rebuffed her offer to help with cooking. Frostrup called Odudu’s response “aggressive”; the reviewer argues that the exchange did not support that description.

segments.title: A loaded description
segments.body: The writer connects the label to a recurring experience for Black women, whose reasonable disagreement can be misread as aggression. The article says Wayne Rooney and Claire Sweeney, who witnessed the exchange, disagreed with Frostrup’s account.

The piece reports that producers had spoken to Frostrup about her language. Although the two women later tried to clear the air, the reviewer says Frostrup did not retract the word, leaving the disagreement unresolved.

content.headline: GTA VI makes everyday routines part of its criminal-world appeal
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI finds unexpected pleasure in everyday routines
content.standfirst: The game’s chores, shopping and care for a pet snake can feel as absorbing as its robberies and car chases. A review essay argues that Rockstar makes routine satisfying by giving players a home and relationships to care about.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI pairs crime with the everyday business of keeping house.

sources.originalTitle: The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine

segments.body: In Grand Theft Auto VI, Jason’s daily tasks include working out, choosing clothes, feeding his pet snake and fixing things around his apartment. The essay finds these routines unexpectedly compelling amid the game’s crime and constant demands from friends and employers.

segments.title: Routine with a reason
segments.body: The writer argues that many games already revolve around completing tasks efficiently, but GTA VI makes those actions pleasurable through its detailed world and tactile feedback. The difference, the essay suggests, is the relationship between Jason and Lucia: daily tasks feel meaningful because the characters depend on one another.

content.headline: GTA VI’s classical radio station pairs Yuja Wang with virtual crime
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s classical station makes Tchaikovsky part of the chaos
content.standfirst: Pianist Yuja Wang hosts Symphony FM in Grand Theft Auto VI, choosing 16 classical works for a world of heists, driving and romance. The review sees the station as an entertaining way to introduce a vast audience to unfamiliar musical worlds.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI, where Yuja Wang hosts a classical music station.

sources.originalTitle: Steal a chopper listening to Liszt! I love how Grand Theft Auto VI went crazy for classical

segments.body: Symphony FM is hosted in the game by real-life pianist Yuja Wang, who selected 16 works for the station. The playlist includes her performances of Ravel and Prokofiev, alongside pieces by composers including Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Sibelius and Mahler.

segments.title: A different soundtrack for the sandbox
segments.body: The essay describes how the classical pieces accompany everything from driving and romance to robberies and violence. Wang’s scripted comments make jokes about classical music’s reputation, while the review argues that the station offers players a route into music beyond the game’s more expected sounds.

The reviewer notes that listeners may debate the choices and catches a mismatch between one spoken introduction and the piece that follows. Even so, the essay sees the station’s scale and reach as an unusual opportunity for classical music within a popular game.

content.headline: Few women reviewed GTA VI, despite its first female lead in decades
content.shortHeadline: Why so few women reviewed GTA VI
content.standfirst: The review count for Grand Theft Auto VI included only six women among 156 critics, according to the article. It argues that this imbalance reflects the wider scarcity and precarity of women in games journalism, as well as a missed chance to hear more perspectives on Lucia.

image.caption: Lucia Caminos, one of the central characters in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?

segments.body: When the review embargo lifted, only six of 156 critics appeared to be women, the article reports. It also cites a survey of editorial teams at major games sites, finding that women made up just over a quarter of the writers counted.

segments.title: A narrow range of voices
segments.body: The writer connects the numbers to media consolidation, job losses, burnout and the particular hostility directed at women, queer and non-white critics. The absence is especially striking, the article argues, because Lucia is the first central female protagonist in the main GTA series in 30 years.

The piece asks what female critics might have brought to discussion of Lucia’s story and the game’s treatment of gender and contemporary America. It leaves open whether the wider audience for GTA VI will lead to more diverse critical coverage in the future.

content.headline: Satellite shorelines reveal metre-scale differences in beach tides
content.shortHeadline: Satellite images reveal sharp differences in beach tides
content.standfirst: A study of 40 years of Pacific shoreline images found tidal heights can vary substantially along a single beach. Mapping those local differences could help improve tide and flood forecasts, especially where gauges are scarce.

image.caption: Satellite measurements found tidal heights differed by almost a metre across a beach in New Zealand.

sources.originalTitle: How a new way of measuring tides could make flood forecasts more accurate

segments.body: Researchers used satellite photographs of shorelines as a measure of tidal height, estimating levels every 100 metres. Existing tide gauges record conditions at a particular spot, while satellite radar measurements typically average across much larger areas.

segments.title: A more local picture
