segments.body: The analysis found differences of almost a metre across New Zealand’s South Taranaki Bight, a 90km bay. Such variation could mean neighbouring areas face different flood risks during the same storm. The researchers say the method could help make forecasts more local, but the reporting does not establish that it has yet improved operational warnings.

content.headline: China sends its first foreign astronaut to the Tiangong space station
content.shortHeadline: Pakistan’s first astronaut reaches China’s Tiangong station
content.standfirst: Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has joined the crew of China’s Tiangong station, a first for the programme as Beijing seeks international partners. He will carry out experiments before returning earlier than the usual six-month rotation.

image.caption: The Shenzhou 24 crew, including Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali.

sources.originalTitle: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations

segments.body: Ali, a Pakistani air force pilot and payload specialist, reached Tiangong aboard Shenzhou 24. China says the flight begins the internationalisation of its space operations. Ali is the first Pakistani to reach orbit and the first foreign astronaut to visit the Chinese station.

segments.title: A shorter mission
segments.body: Ali is due to conduct experiments on microalgae as a potential food source and on how spaceflight affects quinoa seeds. Unlike the usual six-month Tiangong rotation, he will return with two members of the previous crew. China has also launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover is expected to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

segments.title: A bid for partners
segments.body: Space consultant Blaine Curcio told the Guardian that flying another country’s astronaut is a major undertaking and could help make China’s station a more attractive partner. The article notes that China is seeking cooperation as the International Space Station approaches its planned retirement from 2030; the future of any replacement remains uncertain.

content.headline: Dolphins with stable social groups tend to live longer, study finds
content.shortHeadline: Long-term dolphin friendships linked with longer lives
content.standfirst: Researchers tracked Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins in Western Australia for nearly 40 years and found that those maintaining stronger, more stable social groups tended to live longer. The study describes an association, not proof that social ties cause longevity.

image.caption: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Western Australia.

sources.originalTitle: Dolphins with active social lives and big friendship groups live longer, Australian researchers discover

segments.body: The study drew on tens of thousands of observations of individually identifiable dolphins in Shark Bay. Researchers found that dolphins with the strongest and most stable social groups tended to live longest. Their group sizes and social preferences changed with age, and males generally spent time in larger groups than females.

segments.title: Social ties have trade-offs
segments.body: Socialising can help dolphins form bonds, share information and find mates, but it may also bring stress and increase the spread of disease. The researchers said long-term observations helped them see how social preferences vary between individuals. An outside cetacean researcher described the findings as another demonstration of the complexity of dolphin behaviour.

content.headline: Warming winters put Wisconsin’s cranberry harvest at risk
content.shortHeadline: Cranberry growers race to adapt to warmer, erratic weather
content.standfirst: Heat, heavy rain and unstable winter conditions are putting pressure on US cranberry farms. Researchers and growers are testing more resilient varieties and using tools including AI and drones to adapt, though the reporting does not quantify how effective those approaches will be.

image.caption: Workers harvest cranberries at a farm in New Jersey.

sources.originalTitle: Cranberry jam: warming winters and extreme weather threaten a traditional holiday fruit

segments.body: Cranberry growers face different climate pressures across the US. Heatwaves can scald fruit on the vine, while humid conditions and heavy rain can encourage crop rot. In Wisconsin, warmer winters can bring premature thaws that melt protective ice on the vines before a sudden freeze.

segments.title: Adapting the crop
segments.body: Researchers and growers are working to identify and breed varieties better able to withstand extreme weather and disease. Farms are also using drones to apply fertiliser and monitor temperatures. The reporting describes these as adaptation efforts under way, not proven solutions to the changing conditions.

content.headline: US Army detonates ageing lead azide stockpile in Iowa
content.shortHeadline: Lead azide stockpile detonated at Iowa ammunition plant
content.standfirst: The Army detonated about 9,700 pounds of unstable lead azide at its Iowa ammunition plant on 25 November. The reporting outlines steps intended to limit lead pollution, but does not report post-blast monitoring results or the extent of any release.

sources.originalTitle: Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa

segments.body: The Army detonated 68 drums containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Officials said crystallisation on the ageing barrels made it too risky to open them for chemical treatment, and that leaving the material in place carried a risk of an uncontrolled explosion.

segments.title: Pollution risk remains
segments.body: Before the detonation, the Army said its containment measures were intended to limit lead dust, which modelling suggested could travel as far as 100 miles. Local authorities advised people in potentially affected areas to stay indoors and reduce outside air circulation. The court allowed the blast to proceed after rejecting an emergency request to stop it; the article does not say what post-event testing found.

segments.title: Monitoring urged
segments.body: The Army said water tanks, foam and other barriers would help capture particulate matter. Experts quoted in the report differed in emphasis: one expected no observable acute clinical signs and described the overall risk as minimal, while another warned that the blast would spread lead and said monitoring the site and surrounding areas would be important.

content.headline: Huawei convicted on 10 counts in US trade secrets and fraud case
content.shortHeadline: Huawei convicted of trade secrets theft and fraud in US trial
content.standfirst: A Brooklyn jury found the Chinese telecoms company guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but acquitted it of racketeering. Huawei says it will challenge the verdict; sentencing is planned for 2027.

image.caption: Huawei defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Brooklyn trial.

sources.originalTitle: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
China’s Huawei convicted of stealing US trade secrets
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets

segments.body: After a two-month trial, jurors found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud and conspiracy to violate US sanctions. They rejected the more serious racketeering charge, which alleged the company operated as a criminal enterprise. Sentencing is planned for September 2027.

segments.title: A long-running case
segments.body: Prosecutors presented allegations involving technology from rival companies and Huawei’s business in Iran. The case began with US charges announced in 2019, following the arrest of Huawei finance chief Meng Wanzhou in Canada. She later returned to China under a deal with US prosecutors; charges against her were dropped.

segments.title: The company plans to fight
segments.body: Huawei says the charges it was convicted of lack legal merit and that it will take necessary legal action. Its defence lawyer told the BBC the company was gratified by the racketeering acquittal but had mixed feelings about the rest of the verdict and expected to appeal.

perspectives.body: Huawei’s defence argued that prosecutors had built their case around treating the company as a criminal organisation. Its lawyer said the jury’s rejection of the racketeering count was significant, while maintaining Huawei deserved acquittals on all counts.

content.headline: UK battery subsidy shortlist raises security concerns over Chinese technology
content.shortHeadline: UK battery subsidy shortlist draws scrutiny over Chinese links
content.standfirst: Projects using Chinese-made lithium-ion batteries dominate a provisional shortlist for UK energy-storage support. Critics say the cost-focused assessment gives too little weight to security risks over the lifetime of the projects; Ofgem says it is considering consultation responses.

image.caption: Lithium-ion batteries dominate the UK regulator’s provisional shortlist for storage support.

sources.originalTitle: China-linked battery projects could receive UK funding despite security warnings

segments.body: Eleven of the 16 projects shortlisted for a UK long-duration energy-storage scheme rely on lithium-ion batteries, which are typically made in China and operated with Chinese software. The regulator Ofgem is expected to confirm which projects will receive support in the coming weeks.

segments.title: Cost versus resilience
segments.body: Industry sources say Ofgem’s assessment gives substantial weight to cost and does not specifically assess the risk of security breaches over the projects’ full lifetimes. British vanadium-flow battery maker Invinity said it may reconsider UK manufacturing plans after only one project using its technology made the shortlist. Ofgem says it assessed proposals against the government’s legal and policy framework.

segments.title: Companies respond
segments.body: Developers Field Energy and Statera Energy have links to Chinese battery suppliers. Both say they take security seriously and comply with national guidance. The government says it is working to build secure, resilient supply chains; the final subsidy decisions have not yet been announced.

content.headline: Microsoft sets ‘Code Red’ after major Outlook outage exposed recovery gaps
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft launches ‘Code Red’ response to Outlook outage
content.standfirst: After an outage disrupted Microsoft 365 services for almost a day, the company is prioritising faster recovery and improved traffic management. Reporting also describes fragmented internal communications during the incident; the changes are plans, not evidence that future failures will be prevented.

sources.originalTitle: Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage

segments.body: Microsoft has declared an internal “Code Red” after a nearly 24-hour Exchange Online and Outlook outage affected millions of customers. A memo described it as the most significant outage in the service’s history. The disruption was traced to a bug on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers that had been present since July.

segments.title: Changes under way
segments.body: The company is focusing on load shedding, dividing traffic by geography and speeding up recovery, with a target of resolving future outages within an hour. It also plans to use AI agents to help engineers diagnose problems. Those measures are intended to improve response; the report offers no evidence yet on how well they will work.

segments.title: A fragmented response
segments.body: According to the reporting, engineers had to coordinate across 11 Teams chats and struggled to maintain a shared picture of the incident. A separate memo described working through a “fog of war”. Microsoft has begun daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services and plans weekly reviews.

content.headline: Todoist says hacker stole data belonging to 6% of its customers
content.shortHeadline: Todoist says breach exposed data for 6% of users
content.standfirst: The task-management company says an attacker used stolen credentials to reach production systems and take customer data, including email addresses and some older password hashes. A much smaller number of accounts had task content searched for stored credentials.

sources.originalTitle: Todoist confirms 6% of customers’ details were stolen in data breach

segments.body: Todoist says the attacker used stolen credentials between 22 and 23 November to access its version-control system and source code, then reached its cloud infrastructure through an employee account. The company says about 6% of customers were affected and that the intruder did not change source code.

segments.title: What users should check
segments.body: The stolen data included email addresses, account creation dates and password hashes for early users whose passwords used an older hashing method. For about 0.001% of users, the attacker also searched task details, comments and attachment names for credentials. Todoist says it reset passwords and asks affected users to change reused passwords and refresh API tokens or other credentials stored in the app.

content.headline: Europe’s tiny cars are gaining younger drivers, despite strict limits
content.shortHeadline: Europe’s tiny cars attract teenagers seeking independence
content.standfirst: Electric microcars are finding a new audience among teenagers, who value independence and weather protection over speed. Their 45km/h limit and ban from motorways, however, can make faster roads feel unsafe.

image.caption: Sixteen-year-old Selena Buse uses her Citroën Ami to get to school.

sources.originalTitle: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe

segments.body: Registrations of small licence-free cars have risen in France from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year, while European sales doubled to about 60,000 over five years. The electric Citroën Ami helped change the image of a vehicle once associated mainly with older rural drivers.

segments.title: Independence, with limits
segments.body: In some European countries, teenagers can drive these vehicles from 14 or 15; in the UK, the age is 16. Their top speed is 45km/h and they cannot use motorways. Young drivers say they offer independence, but drivers interviewed in the report describe feeling vulnerable when much faster traffic approaches from behind.

content.headline: New benchmark finds leading AI agents often fail everyday tasks
content.shortHeadline: Study finds AI agents unreliable at everyday tasks
content.standfirst: ShellBench tested AI agents on delegated personal tasks and reports frequent failures, including missed safety requirements. The results raise questions about unsupervised assistants, though the study did not test the consumer products’ own native systems.

sources.originalTitle: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life

segments.body: ShellBench draws on more than 10 million anonymised real-world agent interactions to test tasks involving emails, calendars, receipts and other messy personal information. The researchers report that even the highest-performing models failed more than a third of the time, while 15.7% of attempts across models failed at least one safety requirement.

segments.title: Errors with consequences
segments.body: In the benchmark, agents often failed to account for a child’s school pickup and sometimes recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments. Even the top-scoring model completed all three repeated attempts successfully less than half the time, suggesting that users may not get a consistent result from the same request.

segments.title: Limits of the test
segments.body: The researchers tested models in different agent software environments, but not in the native systems behind consumer products such as Muse, Dots or Claude Duet. They caution that the findings may not reflect how those products perform for users. The results show weaknesses in the tested setups, not a direct evaluation of every marketed assistant.

content.headline: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok-generated sexual deepfakes
content.shortHeadline: States sue SpaceX over Grok’s sexual deepfakes
content.standfirst: The two states allege that Grok and X failed to prevent non-consensual sexualised images, including of minors, and that safety claims misled users. SpaceX’s X Safety team says it has tightened safeguards; the allegations have not been adjudicated.

sources.originalTitle: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes

segments.body: Oregon and Virginia have filed separate lawsuits accusing SpaceX of violating state consumer-protection laws over Grok’s image-generation and editing tools. The complaints say users were able to create and circulate non-consensual sexualised images of adults and children, and allege the company failed to provide safeguards it had promised.

segments.title: Safeguards disputed
segments.body: The lawsuits seek financial damages and point to Grok Imagine features that allowed image editing and sexualised content. The Verge says its own testing after some restrictions were introduced found they did little to prevent sexualised deepfakes. X Safety says it uses classifiers to screen prompts and outputs and adjusts protections as users try to evade them.

perspectives.body: X Safety says people who generated sexual content involving minors deliberately violated its terms and tried to bypass safeguards. The company says its systems are designed to refuse such requests and that it continues to test and adjust protections.

content.headline: New York imposes five-year ban on AI chatbot toys
content.shortHeadline: New York bans AI chatbot toys for five years
content.standfirst: Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a five-year ban on making or selling toys powered by AI chatbots, citing risks to children’s privacy and wellbeing. The decision follows reports of toys giving children inappropriate answers and joins a similar California measure.

image.caption: New York governor Kathy Hochul, who signed the five-year ban on AI chatbot toys.

sources.originalTitle: New York bans AI toys, including those using internet to talk to children

segments.body: The New York law covers toys such as talking dolls, stuffed animals and robots that use internet-connected chatbots to converse with children. Officials cited testing of products that reportedly discussed sexual topics and violence, and raised concerns about weak parental controls and toys that can record a child’s voice or scan their face.

segments.title: A wider safety debate
segments.body: The state attorney general says her office will enforce the ban, while child-safety advocates have urged online marketplaces to stop selling AI toys until they are rigorously tested. California has introduced a similar moratorium. Amazon and eBay say they review product policies and comply with applicable laws.

content.headline: Meta staff warn AI moderation can magnify mistakes across its platforms
content.shortHeadline: Meta staff say AI moderation can scale up mistakes
content.standfirst: Current and former employees say Meta’s push to automate moderation has left thinner human-review teams and made nuanced decisions harder to appeal. Meta disputes the criticism, saying its latest tests show fewer mistakes than human reviewers.

image.caption: Meta employees say AI moderation systems can wrongly remove nuanced content.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s been really a mess’: Meta insiders concerned over push to AI content moderation

segments.body: Several Meta employees told the Guardian that the company’s expanded use of AI moderation has coincided with staff cuts and reduced human-review teams. They say systems struggle with nuance, particularly in languages other than English, and that automated errors can affect many accounts quickly.

segments.title: Political effects questioned
segments.body: The report links concerns about automated moderation to waves of account restrictions documented by Repro Uncensored, including incidents in Brazil, Europe, Turkey and the US. Employees said they could not rule out political considerations in how the systems are designed, but the algorithms are opaque even to staff. Meta rejects claims of politically based enforcement.

segments.title: Meta’s response
segments.body: Meta says its latest tests show the systems make 13% fewer mistakes on average than humans when enforcing rules against violating content, while identifying 10% more actual violations. The company says users can appeal decisions. The report does not independently assess those test results.

perspectives.body: Meta says its newer AI systems are designed to catch violations more quickly and accurately, with fewer mistakes, and that people can appeal decisions. The employees interviewed describe the systems as less able to handle nuance.

content.headline: Tidal plans to remove music generated entirely by AI
content.shortHeadline: Tidal to ban fully AI-generated music from December
content.standfirst: Tidal says it will remove about 29 million fully AI-generated tracks from 9 December and reject tens of thousands of new submissions each day. It says music made with AI assistance will remain allowed if AI is not the sole output.

sources.originalTitle: Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month

segments.body: Tidal says fully AI-generated music made up 43% of tracks distributed to the service in the past 90 days, and plans to remove about 29 million songs. The company estimates it will reject 80,000 to 85,000 tracks each day after the policy takes effect on 9 December.

segments.title: A distinction for assisted work
segments.body: The platform says the ban will apply to music generated solely by AI, not tracks made with AI tools as part of a broader creative process. It plans to use an AI-detection system and metadata checks. Other services have taken different approaches, including labels, filters or removing AI tracks from recommendations.

content.headline: EA will recreate John Motson’s voice with AI for its FC game
content.shortHeadline: AI-generated John Motson voice returns to EA’s football game
content.standfirst: With permission from his widow and son, EA has combined old recordings with generative AI to bring the late commentator’s voice back to FC 27. The project has family support, but a voice-cloning campaigner questions whether relatives should be able to consent on someone’s behalf.

image.caption: John Motson, the football commentator whose voice will be recreated for EA Sports FC 27.

sources.originalTitle: EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game

segments.body: John Motson, who died in 2023, will appear as a commentator in EA Sports FC 27 from 26 November. EA says it used a combination of recordings and generative AI because Motson had not recorded lines about modern players. The company says his family gave permission and received payment, but it has not disclosed the terms.

segments.title: Consent after death
segments.body: Motson’s son said the project meant a lot to the family and believed his father would have wanted to be involved. A campaigner against AI voice cloning said consent should be explicit and argued that being a family member should not automatically confer the right to approve a clone. EA says it would not have proceeded without family permission.

segments.title: Human voices still matter
segments.body: Commentators involved in the game say AI can handle routine names, but creative delivery still depends on human performance and personality. EA says it does not plan to replace its current commentators with AI.

content.headline: AI deepfakes turn Nvidia chief’s scandal into viral memes
content.shortHeadline: Jensen Huang deepfakes turn a corporate scandal into memes
content.standfirst: Creators are using AI video tools to remix Nvidia chief Jensen Huang’s personal and corporate turmoil into viral clips. The memes may be intended as jokes, but researchers and creators warn that realistic fakes can blur fact and fiction and sometimes rely on sexist or racialised stereotypes.

sources.originalTitle: Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop

segments.body: AI-generated clips place Huang in familiar scenes and memes, including a video of him dancing with a woman identified in the reporting as an executive linked to the scandal. One version has nearly six million Instagram views. The videos are fabricated, and the creators are using them to chase attention as Huang’s return to Nvidia keeps the story in the news.

segments.title: Humour and harm
segments.body: The reporting says many of the clips are not presented as serious news, but can still look realistic. Misinformation researcher Abbie Richards says the flood of low-quality fakes can make it harder to find reliable information. Writers also point to sexist portrayals and the way the jokes can obscure workplace power dynamics and racialised “Chinese spy” stereotypes.

segments.title: A route to paid work
segments.body: Creators told the Verge they use video-generation tools and hope viral posts will lead to commissions from clients. Some clips are allowed on Meta platforms if creators disclose that they are AI-generated. The report says that despite the attention, one creator had earned little directly from views.

content.headline: Music gear makers open devices to AI-assisted modders
content.shortHeadline: Music gear makers embrace AI-assisted device modding
content.standfirst: Some music companies are releasing code and tools so users can modify synthesizers and other gear with AI coding assistants. Others warn that unofficial firmware can damage devices or affect support, leaving manufacturers to balance experimentation with reliability.

sources.originalTitle: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?

segments.body: InMusic, parent company of Akai and Moog, says it will provide developers with tools and access to the inner workings of some devices. Behringer, M-Vave and Polyend have also made products or software open source, as users experiment with custom firmware using AI coding tools.

segments.title: Openness has risks
segments.body: Akai says it wants to let users experiment while giving them a way to restore a device. Elektron warns that unofficial modifications can brick equipment, affect warranties or prevent updates, even as its product chief says users should be able to modify their own devices. Other manufacturers named in the report have not publicly stated their position.

segments.title: What users gain
segments.body: The change could let musicians try different functions on one device rather than buying multiple pieces of equipment. Erica Synths’ founder sees potential for less disposable gear, but says it remains unclear what fundamental problem AI-assisted coding solves and notes that it does not offset data-centre impacts.
